checks: Integrating over x gives axial density r(z)^(d−1), so the cone mass is B/d. In (u,r) coordinates with x=ru, normalized volume factors as uniform u on [−1,1] and the Beta(d,1) radius law d r^(d−1)dr. The frustum restricts that same radius law to r≥a and loses mass fraction t=a^d. For b≤1 the cone capture condition is r≤H/(B−b), giving the p0 kernel term, and for b>1 the whole ray is captured.

Apply accepted 1f86e3e352aa0225 to each point mass with the same d,H and with 0<U<H. Its cap normalization V0=B/d is constant. As U increases to H, T increases to infinity, t tends to zero, 0≤tw≤t, and the cap and section domains increase to the cone domains up to null sets. The apex is volume-null and, since its margin equals H>0, lies outside every finite-slope section. The signed first moment converges because z is bounded and the section coarea is finite. At s=0 the horizontal section directly gives C0 and M=0.

The kernels (1−b/B)^(−d) and b(1−b/B)^(−d−1) are uniformly bounded for b≤1. Bounded domination proves the cutoff limit and permits averaging the resulting pointwise record identities without any moment restriction on s. Positive slopes give uniform layers with no atom at 1, and the zero layer is the atom at 0. Every finite layer contributes strictly more than half its mass to b≤1, so integrating its positive excess gives v>1/2.

On a compact q-interval inside (0,1), 1−qb has a positive uniform lower bound for 0≤b≤1 and grows uniformly linearly as b tends to −infinity. The first two derivatives are dominated there by constant multiples of |b|^j(1−qb)^(−d−j), j=1,2. Thus e is C² and convex, and e′(a0) equals d times the signed b integral. The factor −H/(Bd) relating it to M/C0 is nonzero, and a0 belongs to (0,1), so stationarity and minimization are equivalent.

Evenness makes the probability of [−1,1] exactly 2v−1 and its conditional mean zero. Jensen on that interval gives the lower bound without centering. At v=1 the whole law is supported there, so e(q) tends to 1 as q decreases to zero and centered minimality gives the upper bound 1.

For k=1−v in (0,1/2), the test q=2k/d belongs to (0,1). The logarithmic derivative in the exponent p≥2 is nonpositive since h(y)=log(1+y)−y/(1+y) has derivative y/(1+y)^2 and global minimum h(0)=0 on (−1,∞). Here y=−2kb/p>−1 for every captured b, including the negative tail. This gives the exponent-two comparison in the stated direction.

For s≥1 the exponent-two primitive (1−kb)^(−1)/k on [−s,1] gives I_k(1/s). For 0<s<1 it gives (1−k²s²)^(−1)≤1/(1−k²)=I_k(1), and the atom at zero contributes 1≤I_k(1). The captured fraction is (1+x)/2 in all cases. Independently, I_k(x)=[x+1−k−k(1−k)/(x+k)]/[2(1−k)], so I_k''=−k/(x+k)^3 and I_k(1−2k)=(1−2k)/(1−k). Jensen then gives the asserted upper bound, with no uniform upper bound on the slopes needed.
